title: ISP Tracking & DNS Privacy Security Checklist
metaDescription: Complete checklist to protect yourself from ISP tracking, DNS monitoring, and data selling. Stop internet provider spying with these privacy steps.
intro: Your internet service provider can see every website you visit, sell your browsing data, and throttle your connection. This comprehensive checklist helps you reclaim your privacy from ISP surveillance through encrypted DNS, secure browsing, and proven privacy tools.

items.task: Switch to encrypted DNS provider (DNS over HTTPS)
items.why: Your ISP can see every website you visit through DNS requests. Encrypted DNS prevents this surveillance and protects your browsing privacy.
items.howTo: Use Cloudflare (1.1.1.1), Quad9 (9.9.9.9), or NextDNS. Enable DNS over HTTPS in your browser settings or router configuration. Test with dnsleaktest.com to verify it's working.

items.task: Enable DNS over HTTPS in your browser
items.why: Browser-level DNS encryption ensures your DNS queries are protected even if your system DNS isn't configured properly.
items.howTo: Chrome: Settings > Privacy > Security > Use secure DNS. Firefox: Settings > Network Settings > Enable DNS over HTTPS. Choose a trusted provider like Cloudflare or Quad9.

items.why: Router configuration protects all devices on your network automatically, including smart devices that can't be configured individually.
items.howTo: Access router admin panel (usually 192.168.1.1). Find DNS settings and enter encrypted DNS servers. Some routers support DNS over TLS - enable if available.

items.why: ISPs often override your DNS settings to maintain tracking capabilities and inject ads or redirect traffic.
items.howTo: In router settings, disable 'Automatic DNS from ISP' or similar options. Set DNS servers to manual mode and use your chosen encrypted DNS provider.

items.why: DNS leaks can expose your browsing activity to your ISP even when using VPNs or encrypted DNS services.
items.howTo: Visit dnsleaktest.com and ipleak.net monthly. Run extended tests to verify your DNS requests aren't leaking to your ISP's servers.

items.why: VPNs encrypt all your internet traffic and hide your browsing activity from your ISP, preventing data collection and selling.
items.howTo: Choose a no-logs VPN like ExpressVPN, NordVPN, or Surfshark. Enable kill switch and DNS leak protection. Connect before browsing to encrypt all traffic.

items.why: HTTPS encrypts your data in transit, preventing ISPs from reading the content of your communications and injecting ads.
items.howTo: Enable HTTPS-only mode in browser settings. Install HTTPS Everywhere extension. Check for the lock icon in address bar before entering sensitive data.

items.task: Use Incognito Browser for sensitive browsing
items.why: Incognito Browser provides built-in privacy features and doesn't store browsing history that could be accessed by ISPs through data requests.
items.howTo: Download Incognito Browser for enhanced privacy features. Use for sensitive searches, banking, and personal browsing to minimize data collection.

items.task: Opt out of ISP data selling programs
items.why: Many ISPs have opt-out programs for data selling, but they're often hidden and require manual action to activate.
items.howTo: Contact your ISP customer service and specifically request to opt out of all data selling, marketing, and analytics programs. Get confirmation in writing.

items.task: Review and limit ISP account permissions
items.why: ISP accounts often have broad data collection permissions enabled by default that extend beyond basic service provision.
items.howTo: Log into your ISP account online. Review privacy settings and disable marketing, analytics, and third-party sharing options. Update preferences monthly.

items.why: Tor provides the highest level of anonymity by routing traffic through multiple encrypted layers, making ISP tracking nearly impossible.
items.howTo: Download official Tor Browser from torproject.org. Use for highly sensitive browsing. Never download files or enable plugins while using Tor.

items.why: Regular speed monitoring helps detect ISP throttling patterns and provides evidence if you need to file complaints.
items.howTo: Use fast.com, speedtest.net, and your ISP's speed test weekly. Test at different times and compare results. Document slower speeds during peak usage.

items.task: Enable VPN to bypass content-based throttling
items.why: ISPs often throttle specific types of traffic like streaming or torrenting. VPNs hide traffic type from ISP analysis.
items.howTo: Use VPN when streaming, downloading, or during activities that experience slow speeds. Compare speeds with and without VPN to identify throttling.

items.why: Traffic analysis allows ISPs to identify and throttle specific activities. Obfuscation makes your traffic appear as regular web browsing.
items.howTo: Enable obfuscation features in your VPN if available. Use traffic shaping tools or proxies that disguise torrent traffic as HTTP traffic.

items.why: Detailed records of throttling help when filing complaints with regulators and can support claims for service credits.
items.howTo: Screenshot speed tests, note times and activities during slow speeds. Keep records of customer service calls about speed issues.

items.why: Net neutrality violations and undisclosed throttling are illegal in many jurisdictions. Complaints can result in action and compensation.
items.howTo: File complaints with FCC (US) or equivalent regulator. Include speed test evidence and documentation. Consider switching ISPs if throttling persists.

items.why: Default router passwords allow ISPs and attackers to access your network settings and potentially monitor your traffic.
items.howTo: Access router admin panel and change default username/password to strong, unique credentials. Enable WPA3 encryption if available.

items.task: Disable ISP remote access to router
items.why: Many ISPs maintain remote access to customer routers for 'support' but this creates privacy and security vulnerabilities.
items.howTo: In router settings, disable remote management, ISP remote access, and automatic firmware updates. Check monthly to ensure settings remain disabled.

items.task: Use your own router and modem
items.why: ISP-provided equipment often includes monitoring capabilities and backdoors that compromise your privacy and security.
items.howTo: Purchase your own cable modem and router. Research compatibility with your ISP. Configure with privacy-focused settings from setup.

items.task: Enable router firewall and intrusion detection
items.why: Firewalls block unauthorized access attempts and intrusion detection alerts you to potential monitoring or attacks.
items.howTo: Enable SPI firewall in router settings. Turn on intrusion detection and logging. Review logs monthly for suspicious activity.

items.why: Firmware updates patch security vulnerabilities that could be exploited by ISPs or attackers to monitor your network.
items.howTo: Check router manufacturer's website monthly for firmware updates. Download and install manually rather than enabling automatic updates.

pro_tips: Use multiple DNS providers for redundancy - configure primary and secondary encrypted DNS servers to maintain privacy if one fails.
Test your privacy setup monthly using tools like dnsleaktest.com, ipleak.net, and browserleaks.com to ensure ISP tracking protection remains active.
Consider using a privacy-focused ISP like ProtonVPN's ISP service or local providers with strong privacy policies if available in your area.
Combine VPN with Tor for maximum anonymity when conducting highly sensitive activities - this creates multiple encryption layers ISPs cannot penetrate.
Monitor your ISP's privacy policy changes by setting up Google Alerts - ISPs often change data collection practices with minimal customer notification.
